The Treaty of Tordesillas. Signed on June 7, 1494. It partitioned the non-European world between Spain and Portugal at the behest of Pope Alexander the Sixth. The treaty drew a meridian line three hundred seventy leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. Portugal got the eastern territories—Africa, India, and Brazil. Spain got the western hemisphere, the Americas. The treaty codified European imperialism and shaped global colonialism for the next four centuries.

The treaty was signed only two years after Columbus's first voyage to the Americas. The papal bull Inter Caetera in 1493 gave Spain dominion over newly discovered lands. Portugal objected. The treaty resolved the dispute by drawing a line and dividing the world. No non-European powers were consulted. The treaty assumed European right to partition the globe. This assumption would undergird colonialism for the next five centuries.

The line of demarcation ran roughly three hundred seventy leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. That's approximately eleven hundred miles. The line was modified by negotiation. Spain claimed all lands west of the line—effectively the entire Americas. Portugal claimed lands to the east. The vague boundary caused centuries of dispute. The line's inexactness allowed Portugal to claim Brazil, which was discovered in 1500 and extends east of the original line. So Portugal got more than the original agreement suggested.

The territorial division gave each power rich spoils. Portugal secured control of Africa, India, and Brazil—the prime sources of spices, gold, and enslaved labour. Spain gained dominion over Central America, South America except Brazil, the Caribbean, and Mexico. These were vast territories with silver, gold, and indigenous populations to exploit.

The treaty excluded France, England, and the Netherlands. This spurred them to colonise unguarded territories and raid Spanish and Portuguese shipping. European colonialism became a competitive scramble, with each power trying to grab what it could.

The treaty facilitated the Atlantic slave trade. African captives flowed to American plantations under the treaty's framework. It drew the geopolitical boundaries—linguistic, cultural, religious—that define Latin America and Africa today.

The Treaty of Tordesillas epitomises the Age of Exploration's hubris. Two Catholic powers, armed with papal authority and possession of the compass and caravel, divided a world they barely knew. The treaty was less a negotiated compromise than a division of spoils between two competitors, excluding rivals and utterly disregarding indigenous peoples. The line proved impossible to enforce precisely in practice. Disputes erupted for centuries, especially over Brazil. The weakness of the demarcation spawned a century of privateering and colonial wars.

Yet the treaty's logic became the template for all European colonialism. The idea was that discovery granted possession, that cartographic division was binding, that indigenous inhabitants had no rights. The languages, religions, and political systems of Latin America and Africa still bear the imprint of which side of the Tordesillas line they fell upon. It is a foundational treaty not because it worked, but because it expressed a principle—European supremacy—that structured the modern world.
